cards.statement: A base-class constraint exposes that base class's public members to generic code.
cards.explanation: A base-class constraint makes its accessible members known while the compiler checks generic code.

cards.statement: A `struct` constraint allows `int?` as a generic type argument.
cards.explanation: The struct constraint admits non-nullable value types. Using int? for that type parameter causes a compiler error.
cards.misconception: Nullable value types satisfy the struct constraint.

cards.statement: A struct with a string instance field satisfies an unmanaged constraint.
cards.explanation: An unmanaged struct has instance fields of unmanaged types. A string instance field prevents it from satisfying the unmanaged constraint.
cards.misconception: A struct qualifies as unmanaged even when it contains a reference-type field.

cards.statement: The `new()` constraint requires a public parameterless constructor on its type argument.
cards.explanation: The compiler checks constructor availability through new() and permits new T() in constrained generic code.

cards.statement: One generic type parameter can have constraints naming several interfaces.
cards.explanation: The compiler checks a candidate type against each interface constraint listed for the parameter.

cards.statement: The compiler accepts `where T : new(), IDisposable` as a valid constraint order.
cards.explanation: The new() constraint follows ordinary interface constraints. where T : IDisposable, new() uses the permitted order.
cards.misconception: The new() constraint has the same placement freedom as interface constraints.

cards.statement: Violating a `notnull` constraint stops compilation with a compiler error.
cards.explanation: With nullable warnings enabled, a notnull violation produces a warning. Compilation proceeds when warnings are not treated as errors.
cards.misconception: A notnull constraint violation produces an ordinary constraint error.

cards.statement: With `where T : class`, generic `==` uses the concrete type argument's overloaded value equality.
cards.explanation: For a type parameter constrained by class, generic == checks reference identity instead of binding the concrete type's overloaded operator.
cards.misconception: A class constraint makes generic == use the concrete type's overloaded equality.

cards.statement: `List<string>` supports an implicit covariance conversion to `List<object>`.
cards.explanation: List<T> is invariant. The compiler rejects an implicit assignment from List<string> to List<object>.
cards.misconception: List<T> gains covariance from the variant interfaces it implements.

cards.statement: The compiler rejects a variance conversion from `Func<int>` to `Func<object>`.
cards.explanation: Generic variance applies to reference-type conversions. A value-type argument such as int stays invariant even in a variant delegate.

cards.statement: In C# 13, `T` constrained by `where T : allows ref struct` can be an ordinary class.
cards.explanation: The anti-constraint adds eligible type arguments; it does not restrict T to ref structs. Generic code still follows ref-safety rules.

cards.statement: In C# 14, `nameof(List<>)` evaluates to the string "List".
cards.explanation: An unbound generic type is a valid nameof operand. Its result contains the simple type name, with the type-argument list and arity omitted.

cards.statement: A class can list several implemented interfaces together in its declaration.
cards.explanation: C# accepts several interface names in a class's base-type list so one class can fulfill multiple contracts.

cards.statement: A matching public instance method supplies an implicit interface implementation.
cards.explanation: A public class method whose signature matches the interface member supplies its implementation through ordinary interface mapping.

cards.statement: A class-typed reference can call an explicit interface method as an ordinary class member.
cards.explanation: An explicit interface implementation is accessed through a reference of the corresponding interface type.
cards.misconception: Explicit implementation adds a method callable through the class's public API.

cards.statement: One public method can implement matching signatures declared by two interfaces.
cards.explanation: When two implemented interfaces declare the same method signature, one matching public class method can serve both.

cards.statement: The compiler accepts interface I { void M(); } interface J : I { } class C : J { }.
cards.explanation: A concrete class implementing a derived interface also supplies implementations for inherited abstract members.
cards.misconception: A derived interface's implementing class owes implementations for its newly declared members alone.

cards.statement: A class-typed reference can call a default method whose implementation comes from its interface.
cards.explanation: An interface's supplied default method is called through an interface-typed reference; it does not become a callable member of the class.
cards.misconception: Classes inherit default interface methods into their callable member set.

source.title: Update interfaces with default interface methods

cards.statement: For an implicit implementation, an interface call uses the class method over the interface's default body.
cards.explanation: A class's matching public implementation replaces the interface's default behavior when code calls through that interface.

cards.statement: An interface stores per-instance values in fields declared in its own body.
cards.explanation: Interface declarations reject instance fields. Instance storage belongs to implementing types.
cards.misconception: Default interface bodies permit per-instance field storage in the interface.

cards.statement: Generic code calls a static abstract interface member through a constrained type parameter.
cards.explanation: The interface constraint makes the static member available through T.Member; the type argument selects its implementation.

source.title: Explore static virtual members in interfaces

cards.statement: The compiler rejects a type that retains a static virtual interface method's default body.
cards.explanation: A static virtual interface method supplies a default implementation. An implementing type can use that body or provide its own.
cards.misconception: A static virtual interface method requires an override like a static abstract method.

source.title: Explore static virtual members in interfaces

cards.statement: C# 13 permits a `ref struct` to implement an interface in its declaration.
cards.explanation: A ref struct can declare interface contracts and supply the matching member implementations.

cards.statement: C# 13 ref structs inherit the default instance implementations of their interfaces.
cards.explanation: A ref struct implementing an interface supplies its own implementations of instance members, including those with default bodies.
cards.misconception: Ref structs can rely on default instance interface implementations as ordinary structs do.

cards.statement: The declaration pattern value is string text matches when value holds a null object reference.
cards.explanation: The string declaration pattern fails for a null input; a null reference has no matching runtime type.
cards.misconception: Declaration patterns accept null for reference types.

cards.statement: An is null pattern invokes the receiver type's overloaded == operator.
cards.explanation: The compiler evaluates is null independently of any user-defined == operator.
cards.misconception: The null pattern uses overloaded equality.

cards.statement: With int x = 15, x is >= 10 and < 20 evaluates to true.
cards.explanation: The and pattern succeeds when the same int input satisfies both relational subpatterns.

cards.statement: With object? value = null, value is { } evaluates to true.
cards.explanation: An empty property pattern succeeds for a non-null input. The null input makes this pattern fail.
cards.misconception: An empty property pattern accepts null.

cards.statement: For a non-null class-typed value with public void Deconstruct(out int x, out int y), the (0, 0) pattern calls it.
cards.explanation: On a non-null class instance, positional matching invokes Deconstruct to obtain the values it tests.

cards.statement: The tuple pattern (0, > 0) matches the tuple (0, 7).
cards.explanation: The pattern compares tuple elements by position: the first matches 0 and the second satisfies > 0.

cards.statement: With object value = "hi", value is var captured gives captured the compile-time type string.
cards.explanation: A var pattern gives its captured variable the input expression's compile-time type, which is object here.
cards.misconception: A var pattern infers the captured value's runtime type.

cards.statement: With object? item = null, item switch { _ => 1 } produces 1.
cards.explanation: The discard arm matches a null input and supplies its result expression's value.

cards.statement: The list pattern [1, .., 3] requires an element between 1 and 3.
cards.explanation: The slice .. matches zero or more elements, so the int array { 1, 3 } matches [1, .., 3].
cards.misconception: A slice pattern requires a nonempty slice.

cards.statement: An int n when n > limit => 1 switch arm permits a local variable limit as the comparison threshold.
cards.explanation: A when guard evaluates a Boolean expression after pattern matching and can refer to a runtime value in scope.

cards.statement: With int x = 5, x switch { > 0 and < 10 => 1, > 3 => 2, _ => 0 } produces 2.
cards.explanation: A switch expression selects its first matching arm. For x = 5, the > 0 and < 10 arm yields 1 before the later > 3 arm is considered.
cards.misconception: A later matching switch arm replaces the earlier result.

cards.statement: With int x = 2, x switch { 1 => "one" } throws SwitchExpressionException at runtime.
cards.explanation: A non-exhaustive integer switch produces a compiler warning. An uncovered input throws System.Runtime.CompilerServices.SwitchExpressionException.

cards.statement: Array.Resize can grow the existing array instance when the requested length increases.
cards.explanation: When the size changes, Array.Resize allocates a replacement array and copies the existing elements into it.
cards.misconception: Array.Resize changes an array instance's length.

cards.statement: Setting a List<T>'s Capacity to a larger value adds elements to its Count.
cards.explanation: Capacity reserves element storage. Increasing it leaves Count unchanged; Count tracks the elements actually in the list.
cards.misconception: Reserved list slots count as stored elements.

cards.statement: List<T>.Clear() removes the elements while preserving the list's Capacity.
cards.explanation: Clear sets Count to zero and retains the allocated capacity for reuse.

cards.statement: An IEnumerable<T> value represents a collection that stores its elements in memory.
cards.explanation: IEnumerable<T> defines an enumeration contract, not a requirement to hold a materialized collection.
cards.misconception: IEnumerable<T> guarantees stored collection data.

cards.statement: foreach visits a one-dimensional array's elements in increasing index order.
cards.explanation: C# array enumeration starts at index zero and progresses toward the last element.

cards.statement: Calling a synchronous iterator method returns a sequence before code in its body runs.
cards.explanation: The iterator body begins executing when enumeration advances, rather than when the method returns its sequence.

cards.statement: After a yield return, the next iterator advance resumes just after that yield return.
cards.explanation: An iterator preserves its execution position while the caller handles a yielded element.

cards.statement: Executing yield break transfers iterator execution to the code after its surrounding loop.
cards.explanation: yield break ends the current enumeration. Code after the surrounding loop is not the continuation target.
cards.misconception: yield break behaves like a loop's break statement.

cards.statement: In C# 12, ReadOnlySpan<int> values = [1, 2] initializes a span containing those elements.
cards.explanation: Collection expressions convert to arrays, List<T>, Span<T>, ReadOnlySpan<T>, and supported collection interfaces.

cards.statement: In C# 12, IEnumerable<int> xs = [GetValue()] delays GetValue() until xs is enumerated.
cards.explanation: A collection expression evaluates its elements while constructing the collection, including for an IEnumerable<T> target.
cards.misconception: An IEnumerable<T> target makes a collection expression lazy.

cards.statement: In C# 12, [..source] reads the values produced by source to construct its destination.
cards.explanation: A spread element contributes the source's elements to the new collection. Its input must support foreach enumeration.

cards.statement: In C# 12, void Log(int[] values = [1, 2]) declares a valid optional-parameter default.
cards.explanation: Collection expressions are not compile-time constants, even with constant elements. The compiler rejects them as optional-parameter defaults.
cards.misconception: Constant collection elements make the collection expression a constant default.
